imageCaption: A museum hallway where paintings seem to exist in multiple moments of completion simultaneously—some portraits half-finished, some fully rendered, some aging in real-time while others reset to their original state.
text:
The museum was experiencing an identity crisis.

This was the conclusion Aaliyah arrived at approximately three minutes after they'd stepped through the entrance of the Museo de Arte, located in the heart of Old San Juan's glitch zone. The problem wasn't that the museum was in two places at once, though it technically was. The problem was that it was in multiple stages of completion at the same time, which was somehow worse.

The first floor existed as it had been built—wooden beams, stone walls, colonial architecture rendered in careful historical preservation. The second floor was actively being constructed. The third floor was already crumbling into architectural dissolution, slowly returning to whatever it had been before humans had the idea to turn it into a museum. And the fourth floor, which should not have existed in a four-story building, was somehow both under renovation and fully restored and dreaming about being something else entirely.

"This is recursive," Aaliyah said aloud, because saying impossible things was becoming her primary form of coping mechanism. "The museum is existing in its own history and future simultaneously. It's a building that's aware it's a building."

Rosa had come with them, apparently having decided that family tourism was now her responsibility. She was walking through the first-floor galleries with the calm demeanor of someone who'd spent the past hundred days accepting that reality had become negotiable.

"The museum was built in 1835," Rosa said, reading from a placard that kept flickering between English, Spanish, and what might have been Portuguese. "But it was a fortress in 1765. And before that, it was a private residence in 1592. And before that, it was a space the Taíno people used for gathering. And before that, it was just earth. The building knows all of that. It's having difficulty choosing which one to be."

Elijah was delighted by this revelation in the specific way he was delighted by most temporal impossibilities—with the kind of uncomplicated joy that suggested that buildings having existential crises was completely reasonable.

"Can I see the old parts?" he asked.

"You're seeing them," Aaliyah said, pointing to a wall that was simultaneously solid stone and flickering translucent, revealing older architecture underneath. "Look. You can see the layer beneath."

The museum director appeared—a woman who looked like she was made of patience and compromise, which was probably the only way to maintain mental health while working at a building that couldn't decide what era it wanted to exist in.

"We've closed the upper floors," she said to the family with the specific resignation of someone who'd made this announcement seventeen times today. "The recursion is too pronounced. Visitors keep ascending stairs only to discover they're descending. Three people got stuck in what might have been 1765 for twenty minutes before we managed to guide them back to 2026. One of them is still not entirely convinced about the year."

"How long has it been like this?" Luisana was already taking notes, her journalist instincts overriding her tourist sensibilities. This was how she processed moments—by documenting them, turning them into narrative. "Since the Cascade started?"

"Since yesterday morning," the director said. "Yesterday the museum was normal. Boring, even. Completely committed to being a modern building that happened to contain colonial artifacts. And then—" She gestured at the walls, which were currently showing a clear stratification of time. "This. The museum decided it wanted to be honest about all the versions of itself."

Aaliyah felt that specific click in her understanding—the moment when a glitch suddenly made sense not as a disaster but as information.

"It's not broken," she said. "It's confessing."

"Confessing what?" Anthony asked. He'd been examining a painting that existed in what appeared to be multiple states of completion. In one layer it was a portrait of a colonial officer. In another layer it was a portrait of a resistance fighter. The same face, painted twice, occupying the same canvas.

"Confessing that it was built on top of something else," Aaliyah said slowly. "And that something else matters. San Juan was built on the Taíno islands. And then it was colonized. And then there was resistance. And all of that happened in the same place, and the museum just decided it was going to be honest about holding all those moments at once instead of choosing one official history."

Sully released three short barks.

"Minor glitch," Elijah translated. "But it's anchoring itself. It's looking for the frequency to stabilize it."

Luisana was watching her daughter with an expression that suggested she was witnessing something important and was going to remember every detail of it. "You're saying the buildings know. The city knows. They're confessing what they've been holding this whole time."

"The Cascade isn't breaking things," Aaliyah said. "It's making things honest about being multiple things at once."

Rosa nodded slowly. "The museum is like the city. The city is like us. We all exist in multiple moments and we've been pretending we don't. The frequency just makes it impossible to pretend anymore."

The director was listening to this with an expression that suggested she was either having a revelation or experiencing a complete mental breakdown, and Aaliyah respected her commitment to remaining ambiguous about which one it was.

"So what do we do?" the director asked. "Close permanently? Demolish? Burn it down?"

"You let it be honest," Luisana said. She was already moving through the galleries, genuinely seeing them—not as a tourist but as a witness. "You create tours of the layers. You teach people that this building is a time machine, but not because science made it one. Because it's always been one, and now it's finally admitting it."

Anthony was taking photos of everything—not the neat, composed kind of photos that tourists took, but chaotic shots that captured the layering of time, the moments existing on top of each other like geological strata. He was collecting this the way he collected license plates—evidence that he'd been here, proof that multiple truths had intersected in this specific place.

And above them, just visible through the ceiling of the first floor (which was simultaneously showing the floorboards of the second floor), the blue butterfly passed through—Ida, apparently deciding that museums full of honest history deserved acknowledgment.

Sully's three short barks shifted into something longer, more satisfied.

The glitch was stabilizing.

Aaliyah could feel it—the way the walls were settling into their acceptance of existing in multiple moments. The museum was learning to hold its own history without fighting. And in doing that, it was teaching the city something, which would teach the frequency something, which would make it possible for the next glitch to become stable too.

"We're teaching the world permission," Elijah said quietly to no one in particular. He was holding a small stone he'd found in a corner—Taíno era, probably, though there was no way to verify that without radiocarbon dating. "Permission to be all your different selves at the same time."

Rosa squeezed his shoulder. "Your Abuela Ida would be proud of you."

And Aaliyah realized, watching her family move through a museum that was confessing its own history, that this was what the journey actually was. Not a travel adventure. Not a race to Curaçao. Not even a quest to fix the Cascade.

It was a family teaching the entire world how to hold multiple truths without choosing which one was real.

It was permission, moving through the broken places, teaching them how to be whole by admitting they'd never been just one thing in the first place.
